meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In questions of science, the authority of a thousand is not worth the humble reasoning of a single individual'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Galileo — from his third letter on sunspots, 1612. The familiar English wording comes from Arago’s 1859 Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Galileo’s, from the third of his letters on sunspots (December 1612). This particular English sentence is François Arago’s rendering, which we read verbatim in Arago’s Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men (1859) ↗. A literal translation of Galileo’s Italian reads quite differently.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Third letter on sunspots, to Mark Welser
François Arago, Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men (1859), in the eulogy of Laplace
Robert Grant, Baden Powell and W. H. Smyth

source.excerpt: A philosopher, whose name is associated with immortal discoveries, said to his audience who had allowed themselves to be influenced by ancient and consecrated authorities, “Bear in mind, Gentlemen, that in questions of science the authority of a thousand is not worth the humble reasoning of a single individual.” Two centuries have passed over these words of Galileo without depreciating their value, or obliterating their truthful character.
trail: We read the sentence in the source itself: Project Gutenberg’s text of Arago’s Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men, first series ↗ carries it word for word, inside the eulogy of Laplace, and credits it to Galileo.

Wikiquote &↗ files it as a variant translation of the third letter on sunspots (December 1612), giving the page as 365 of the Arago volume, and prints the Italian alongside: “sì perché l’autorità dell’opinione di mille nelle scienze non val per una scintilla di ragione di un solo”.

The same Wikiquote entry gives Stillman Drake’s 1957 literal translation of the Italian — “in the sciences the authority of thousands of opinions is not worth as much as one tiny spark of reason in an individual man” — which is visibly a different sentence from the one in circulation.
source.cutTag: Arago, Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men (1859)
source.excerptNote: Arago is writing about Laplace, and reaches for Galileo to make his point. Note that he presents the line as spoken to “his audience”; Galileo’s actual text is a written letter. The popular quotation also inserts a comma after “science”, which Arago’s text does not have.

source.rightsNote: Both layers are clear. Galileo’s 1612 Italian is long in the public domain, and the English wording quoted here comes from an 1859 translation ↗ — published well before 1931, and distributed by Project Gutenberg as a public-domain text. Unusually for a translated quotation, the words people actually repeat are themselves free to reuse.

author.name: Galileo Galilei
author.heading: About Galileo Galilei
author.bio: Galileo Galilei spent 1612 and 1613 in a public quarrel about sunspots — whether they were on the Sun, and therefore whether the heavens were perfect and unchanging. He held that they were, and that the question was settled by looking rather than by counting authorities. The letters he wrote on the subject are among the first pieces of experimental argument addressed to a general readership.

copyAttribution: "In questions of science the authority of a thousand is not worth the humble reasoning of a single individual." — Galileo Galilei, third letter on sunspots to Mark Welser, December 1612. This English wording is François Arago’s, from Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men (1859), where it reads "Bear in mind, Gentlemen, that in questions of science the authority of a thousand is not worth the humble reasoning of a single individual." Stillman Drake’s literal translation of the Italian reads differently.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Galileo really did write this, and the sentiment is exactly his. But the sentence in circulation is not a translation of what he wrote so much as a nineteenth-century Frenchman’s paraphrase of it.

items.why: The familiar English is Arago’s, from his 1859 Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men. Drake’s literal 1957 translation of the same Italian reads “in the sciences the authority of thousands of opinions is not worth as much as one tiny spark of reason in an individual man”.
Arago stages it as a philosopher addressing “his audience”. Galileo wrote it in a letter, to Mark Welser, in December 1612 — there was no audience and no speech.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Galileo’s argument; genuinely Arago’s sentence ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sunspot letters of 1612 were Galileo’s first public argument that the heavens change — that the Sun itself is blemished and turning. His opponents answered with authorities: Aristotle had said otherwise, and a great many learned men agreed with Aristotle.

His reply is the principle the whole scientific method rests on, and it is why Arago reached for it two centuries later to defend Laplace: a thousand people agreeing is not evidence. One person’s reasoning, checked, is.
detailsBody: Arago (1786–1853) was a physicist and, briefly, a French head of state; his biographical eulogies of scientists were widely read and translated, which is how a French rendering of Galileo’s Italian became the standard English quotation.
context.pull: A thousand people agreeing is not evidence. One person’s reasoning, checked, is.

Wikiquote files this wording as a variant translation of Galileo’s third letter on sunspots (December 1612), sourced to Arago 1859 p. 365, and prints both the Italian and Drake’s 1957 literal translation.
